I've been working my network on this one, and the picture coming out of the FOMC is about as clear as it gets — but let me fill one gap before I commit.

Let me lay out what I'm seeing.

The public narrative is still half-stuck in the 2024–25 cutting mindset. The people actually inside the building have moved on. Kevin Warsh took the chair in May, and everything I'm hearing from the district-bank and Board side is that this is a deliberate, hawkish operator who wants fewer votes and longer deliberation windows — the announcement that the FOMC will convert some 2027–28 meetings into strategy-only sessions with no rate vote tells you the institutional wind is blowing toward "hold and think," not "cut and go." That is a behavioral signal, not a data point.

Now the numbers underneath the behavior. The March 2026 statement pegged the range at 3.50–3.75%. The September SEP median for end-2026 came in at 4.1% — a full 0.3 points higher than June, and 0.5 higher for both 2027 and 2028. When a committee revises its own path up that sharply, in that short a window, it is not preparing to cut. It's telling you it got behind on inflation and is trying to catch up. Multiple sell-side desks are openly positioning for a 25-basis-point *hike* into year-end, not a cut. I've heard the same from two fixed-income PMs who talk directly to the New York desk — nobody in that room is expecting an easing move in December.

The stuff that's messy on the surface: the iShares piece cites a 3.2% longer-run median versus the FRED 4.1% end-of-year, and the Charles Schwab illustration shows 3.50–3.75% with a 78% hold probability. That's an *example* built around a generic range, not a live read — I discount it. The behavioral and projection evidence all points one direction.

And think about what a cut would require. Warsh's Fed, with inflation still above target by its own admission, and with a dot plot that just ratcheted *up* twice, would have to reverse course four weeks after hiking expectations hardened. Chair credibility is the scarcest asset at the Fed right now. Cutting in December would torch the signal the committee just spent two meetings building.

What would move me? If I heard that November CPI printed a genuine negative surprise and that two or three voting governors had flipped dovish in private, I'd shade my number up. If the October minutes revealed a real split and a Warsh who's lost the room — that raises uncertainty but not the hike-to-cut swing. Neither of those is what I'm hearing on the ground. The on-the-ground read is a committee that is far more worried about being too loose than too tight.

So: a cut at the 9 December meeting is a low-probability event. I'd put it in the single digits to low teens — there's always room for the data to genuinely crack and force their hand, but the behavioral and projection evidence is stacked hard against it.

The question asks whether the Fed cuts on 9 December — but the more important move is to check whether the system I'm modelling is even in a cutting regime. It isn't. The September 2026 SEP has the median year-end fed funds projection at 4.1%, up 0.3 percentage points from June. That's not a committee drifting toward easing; that's a committee that has been marking its dots *up* through 2026. The March statement put the range at 3.50–3.75%, and if the dots now sit near 4.1%, the path from March to December runs through hikes, not cuts. Asking whether they cut in December is asking whether the system reverses its own recently-established regime in a single meeting. That's a phase transition, and phase transitions need a trigger, not a trend.

Trace the feedback loops. Start with the supply side: oil disruptions — tankers struck by mines in the Gulf — feed energy prices, feed headline CPI, feed inflation expectations. Expectations are the reinforcing loop that matters most. Once expectations start to migrate upward, the Fed's response function steepens: a small inflation surprise produces a disproportionately larger policy response because the cost of unanchoring is asymmetric. A hawkish chair will not cut into that. Kevin Warsh has spent his first months restructuring the committee's rhythm — fewer rate-setting votes, more strategic deliberation. Institutional inertia is a real variable in this model. Committees that have just reorganised their decision cadence and just raised their dots do not pivot eight weeks later on the strength of one payrolls print.

Now the other direction. "And then what?" — suppose the labour market cracks between the October 28 meeting and December 9. That's the only plausible cut pathway: a fast enough deterioration in payrolls that overrides inflation concerns. But look at the information bandwidth between those two dates. One CPI report, one employment report. Two data points cannot flip a committee whose median dot just moved up. Central banks pivot at December meetings only when they've pre-signalled through October and November speeches — the signalling loop has to close first. I see no evidence in the record of that signalling.

There's also a second-order consideration that cuts against the cut: if the committee hikes in October to 4.00–4.25%, December becomes a natural hold — the dot plot is satisfied, and they sit still. If they held in October at 3.75–4.00%, December is more likely the hike that delivers the 4.1% median than a cut. Either branch of the tree terminates in "not a cut." That's what makes this a robust prediction rather than a close call: the decision tree converges.

The scenario that would change my mind is a credit event — a funding-market dislocation, a sharp equity drawdown forcing a financial-stability response, or a payrolls number negative enough to dominate the inflation signal. That's a tail, and tails are what my confidence range should price, not what should drive the central forecast.

What would move my estimate: the December SEP dot for year-end 2026 (if it stays at 4.1%, cut odds collapse to near zero); the tone of the October 28 statement and any dissents for easing; the next two CPI prints; and any evidence of emergency-style intermeeting signalling. Absent those, the system's own momentum points away from a December cut.

My call: no cut on December 9. The regime, the dots, the chair's preferences, and the information bandwidth between now and then all point the same direction.

That is not a man building toward a December cut.

Now here's where I get contrarian about the contrarians. The lazy take going into this meeting is some version of "inflation is sticky, Warsh is a hawk, the Fed holds." Fine. But the question isn't hold versus cut in the abstract — it's whether the *lower and upper bounds both come down* at the December meeting specifically. And the thing nobody is pricing carefully is the SEP asymmetry: if the September dot plot had year-end 2026 at 4.10%, and the actual range is 3.50–3.75%, there is a gap between projection and reality that either closes through hikes or through a rewrite of the projections. Either way, the base case for December is a hold, not a cut. The crowd that assumes "December is a live cut meeting because that's when the Fed usually moves" is importing a 2024–2025 playbook into a hawkish Warsh regime.

But let me steelman the cut case, because I don't want to be reflexively bearish. Three things could force a cut. First, the October 28 meeting just happened — if the committee held but the statement language softened materially, December could be the deliverable. Second, if the labor data in the November payrolls and CPI prints (released before December 9) deteriorates hard, a chair who prizes "information-rich intervals" might actually use the December meeting as the moment to move, precisely because he's been holding. Third, the SEP median of 4.10% could reflect a minority of hawks dragging the median, with the actual committee closer to neutral — medians hide dispersion, and dispersion is exactly where a contrarian should look.

My problem with all three: they all require data we don't have, and the structure of the question rewards the base rate. Warsh's entire institutional project — spacing out meetings, reserving strategy sessions, resisting the "twitchy" Fed — points toward fewer moves, not a December surprise cut. A chair who just announced he's *reducing* the frequency of rate-setting decisions is signaling that he wants to sit still more, not less. Cutting in December, the same month he's showcasing a longer-horizon framework, would undercut the very story he's telling.

The consensus, as best I can reconstruct it from the stale FedWatch fragments and the SEP, is roughly a 70–80% hold with a modest cut tail. I'm not going to fight the hold — I'm going to fight the *cut tail* being too fat. My contrarian claim is narrower and more defensible: the probability of an actual cut at this specific meeting is lower than the market's residual ~20–25% implies, because the market is still anchored to a "December = cut" seasonal heuristic and to a September SEP that was revised *upward*, not downward. When the dot plot moves up and the market still prices a cut tail, that gap is the mispricing.

What would change my mind? A dovish October 28 statement, a visible crack in the labor market in the November payrolls, or a Fed speaker explicitly pre-committing to December. Absent one of those, I'm on the "no cut" side with real conviction, and I'd put the cut probability in the low-to-mid teens — not zero, because tail risk lives in the data, but well below where the residual market odds sit.
